reason: The wording is right; the named edition is not the one that was read. Project Gutenberg 4399, the verifier's only witness, is not the Frank Shay 1920 first edition. Its contents run First Fig, Second Fig, Recuerdo, Thursday, To the Not Impossible Him, Macdougal Street, The Singing-Woman from the Wood's Edge, She Is Overheard Singing, The Prisoner, The Unexplorer, Grown-up, The Penitent, Daphne, Portrait by a Neighbor, Midnight Oil, The Merry Maid, To Kathleen, To S. M., The Philosopher, then a section of Four Sonnets, and the ebook's own note says it contains several poems not included in earlier editions. The identical contents are transcribed at the Celebration of Women Writers from the Harper and Brothers printing of 1923, copyright 1922. The 1920 Shay chapbook is the short first edition without the sonnets. So the citation names an edition nobody opened, which is the same defect the March Montaigne and Nietzsche lines were corrected for. The poem is certainly in the 1920 book and its four lines are stable across printings, so this is a correction, not a kill: either name the expanded text that was read, or open a 1920 scan and say so. Everything else holds. Gutenberg prints My candle burns at both ends; / It will not last the night; / But ah, my foes, and oh, my friends-- / It gives a lovely light!, with the double hyphen for the printed em dash and lines 2 and 4 indented; the quotation matches word for word and stop for stop, ends in an exclamation mark, uses no straight double quote, and keeps the four line breaks. Millay is not banned, not at cap, not shipped, and opens like nothing shipped (shipped.js clean). Poetry is the form. The source leads with the name, has no dash and is inside 140.
betterCitation: Edna St. Vincent Millay, First Fig, the whole poem, A Few Figs from Thistles (Harper and Brothers, 1922)
